one_liner: Statically typed Go expression language compiled to bytecode; about 1.3x faster than cel-go on a small boolean rule.
what_it_does: Expr compiles a short, side-effect-free expression (comparisons, boolean logic, membership, builtins such as all, filter and map, calls to Go functions) against a Go environment (a struct or a map) and then evaluates it many times. expr.Compile(src, expr.Env(env), options...) type-checks the source against the env and returns a *vm.Program; expr.Run(program, env) evaluates it. It is a rule and filter language with its own syntax, not a CEL implementation and not a general scripting language.
how_it_is_fast: A type checker infers static types from the env, so the compiler emits specialised opcodes: OpLoadFast for map[string]any lookups, OpEqualInt and OpEqualString, and OpCallTyped for functions whose signature is in a generated list, which avoids reflect.Value.Call. An AST optimizer folds constants, turns 'in' over a constant int or string array into a set lookup, and fuses builtins (filter+map, len(filter) into count, sum over ranges and arrays). The VM is a single switch loop over a []Opcode with an []any stack.
when_to_use: Business rules, feature flags, filters and access policies compiled once and evaluated many times against Go structs or maps; the README lists Argo, OpenTelemetry Collector, CoreDNS and KEDA as users.
When type errors in user-written rules should surface at compile time against your Go env type rather than at run time.
Collection predicates over Go slices: map(array, # * 2) on 100 ints took 4,695 vs 24,421 ns/op for cel-go (about 5.2x, derived from page data).

Evaluating untrusted expressions on v1.17.7 or later: evaluation is documented as always terminating, and there is a per-run memory budget (DefaultMemoryBudget 1e6) and a compile-time AST node cap (DefaultMaxNodes 1e4).
Pure-Go builds that want no dependencies: go.mod has no require lines and declares go 1.18.
when_not_to_use: Inputs that are protobuf messages, or expressions that must also run outside Go: franchb/cel-go-benchmarks (linux/amd64, expr v1.8.9 vs cel-go v0.6.0 with OptOptimize and a custom Activation) measured cel-go at 123 ns/op vs Expr at 186 ns/op on one field comparison.
Anything that needs state, side effects or loops: Expr is side-effect-free by design; use goja, Tengo or a Lua engine.

Versions before 1.17.7 with untrusted data or expressions: CVE-2025-68156 (unbounded recursion in flatten, min, max, mean and median crashes the process on deeply nested or cyclic data; fixed in 1.17.7) and CVE-2025-29786 (parser memory exhaustion on huge input; fixed in 1.17.0).
Hot paths that call methods on a struct env: in issue #734 a user measured 365.2 ns/op for a struct-env method vs 48.26 ns/op for a function in a map env and 60.49 ns/op for expr.Function.

integration.thread_safety: Not documented in the files read. expr.Run creates a fresh vm.VM on every call, so concurrent runs of one Program do not share VM state; a reused vm.VM holds per-run state (stack, ip, memory) and should stay on one goroutine.

gotchas: expr.Run allocates a new vm.VM per call; hot loops can reuse a vm.VM (the repo has a Benchmark_expr_reuseVm case), one per goroutine.

Runs that build large arrays or maps (ranges, map, sort) fail once they exceed the 1e6 memory budget, and generated expressions above 10,000 AST nodes are rejected at compile time; raise these with vm.VM.MemoryBudget and expr.MaxNodes.
Go functions whose signature is not in the generated FuncTypes list are called through reflection (the OpCall path); declare hot functions with expr.Function or a matching signature.

Harness caveats in the comparison repo (no flaw found that inflates Expr's lead): single runs at -benchtime=20s with no -count, mid-2023 versions (expr v1.13.0 under the old github.com/antonmedv/expr path, cel-go v0.17.1), and cel-go programs built without cel.EvalOptions(cel.OptOptimize). goja and otto receive their variables once via vm.Set before the loop, while Expr, cel-go and govaluate are passed the params map on every iteration, which favours the JavaScript engines. Results are checked only after the timed loop.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Expr over goja, Tengo or GopherLua when the job is a single side-effect-free rule or filter evaluated many times: on the same boolean rule it is about 2x faster than goja (70.27 vs 146.2 ns/op), and it adds compile-time type checks and termination guarantees. Use those siblings when scripts need statements, state or loops.
verified_claims_summary: In the Expr author's comparison repo (Apple M2, go test -bench=. -benchtime=20s, one run, Go toolchain not stated, mid-2023 library versions), a precompiled boolean rule over a four-key map took 70.27 ns/op in Expr vs 91.27 in cel-go (about 1.3x) and 146.2 in goja, and map over 100 ints took 4,695 vs 24,421 ns/op (about 5.2x, derived from page data). A separate 2020-era benchmark with protobuf input and an optimised cel-go program shows the reverse: cel-go 123 vs Expr 186 ns/op.
status_note: Active (last commit 2026-07-07, 8k stars, MIT, no dependencies) and widely embedded (the README lists Google Cloud, Uber, Argo and OpenTelemetry Collector); use v1.17.7 or later to get both 2025 denial-of-service fixes.
